title: Pomade vs Clay vs Wax: Which Product for Which Cut
hero_alt: Small round metal product tins stacked on a plain surface
card_text: Shine and slick, matte and texture, or something in between. What each product type does and the cuts it suits.
lede: Pomade, clay and wax differ in finish and hold. Pomade gives shine and a smooth, combed look, which suits slick backs and side parts. Clay gives a matte, natural finish with strong hold and texture, which suits crops and textured fringes. Wax sits in between, with a soft shine and flexible hold for short styles you want to rework during the day. Choose by the finish your cut needs, then by how much hold your hair needs.
Here's what each type does, which cuts it suits, and how to use any of them. Product types only, no brands.

seo.title: Pomade vs Clay vs Wax: Which for Which Cut | Carlsbad, NM
seo.description: Pomade vs clay vs wax: shine and hold vs matte texture, and which product type suits a slick back, crop or fringe. From a Carlsbad, NM barber.

blocks.heading: Shine and slick.
paragraphs: Pomade gives hair a shiny, polished finish and lets you comb it into clean lines. Oil-based pomades hold longer but take more washing to get out. Water-based ones rinse out easily and can be restyled with a splash of water.
It's the natural match for a slick back or a combed side part, where the shine is part of the look.
Pomade can feel heavy on short, fine hair, and oil-based types can leave the scalp greasy if you overdo them. It does its finest work on hair with enough length to comb.

blocks.heading: Matte and texture.
paragraphs: Clay dries to a matte, nearly shine-free finish and gives hair grip and body. It makes hair look thicker and keeps pieces separated instead of clumped together.
That makes it a common pick for textured crops and forward styles, where the goal is natural movement. It also tends to suit fine hair, because it adds body without much weight.
Clay can feel stiff if you use too much, and some people find it dries the hair a little. Working it into slightly damp hair makes it easier to spread.

blocks.heading: Somewhere in between.
paragraphs: Wax has a light to medium shine and a softer hold that never sets hard, so you can push the hair around again later in the day.
It works on short to medium styles and for defining individual pieces, like the front of a fringe.
Wax can feel tacky between your fingers and sometimes takes more washing to remove than water-based products. Warming it fully between your palms avoids clumps.

blocks.heading: Pomade, clay, wax.
rows: Can take more than one wash

blocks.heading: Less than you think.
blocks.lead: The habits don't change with the tin.
paragraphs: Very short hair often needs nothing at all. A buzz or a skin-short crop looks fine straight out of the towel.
For everything else, whatever type you choose:
bullets: Start with a pea-sized amount. Add more only if you need it.
Warm it between your palms until it's spread thin.
Work it in from the back to the front so the front doesn't get the biggest share.
Clay and wax usually go on towel-dried hair; pomade can go on damp or dry hair for different levels of shine.
Wash it out regularly so it doesn't build up on the scalp.

items.q: Is clay or pomade better for short hair?
items.a: Clay for a natural, textured look; pomade for a neat, shiny one. It depends on the cut.

items.q: What's the difference between pomade and wax?
items.a: Pomade is shinier and combs into clean lines. Wax is softer, less shiny and easier to rework during the day.
Paste sits between clay and wax: a soft, low-shine finish with medium hold. It works on many short and medium cuts.

items.q: Which product suits a textured fringe?
items.a: Usually a matte clay or a light wax, to keep the pieces separated.
